Newly hatched neonates of the waterflea Sida crystallina are released into the water column after completing embryonic development within the brood chamber. At birth, these individuals measure a mere 0.034 centimeters [Lb = 0.034 centimeters] in body length, a size that places them among the smaller newborn cladocerans relative to their adult dimensions. This initial length is critical for early filter-feeding success on suspended bacteria and small phytoplankton. Laboratory cultures maintained at a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] demonstrate that the mean age at birth is 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days], a developmental period that reflects the species' moderately fast embryogenesis under these thermal conditions. The interval between successive molts at this temperature is approximately 3.9 days, which tightly regulates the pace of somatic growth and reproductive cycling. Feeding begins almost immediately after release, with neonates using their specialized thoracic appendages to create feeding currents that draw in particulate organic matter.

As juveniles progress through successive instars, they undergo a steady increase in body length, a pattern typical of cladoceran growth that follows a stepwise trajectory punctuated by ecdysis. By the time individuals reach the point of sexual maturation, their total length approaches 0.25 centimeters [Lp = 0.25 centimeters], a size threshold that marks a significant physiological transition toward reproductive competence. This milestone is accompanied by substantial changes in body composition, including the development of the brood chamber in females. The dry weight at puberty has been measured at 0.00003116 grams , reflecting the accumulation of somatic and gonadal tissue necessary to support egg production. This value was derived from gravimetric analyses of individuals sampled precisely at the onset of the first instar bearing a visible ovarian anlage. The attainment of this body mass is energetically demanding and depends heavily on the quality and abundance of available food resources, particularly during the late juvenile stages.

Fully grown adult females of Sida crystallina exhibit a maximum total body length of 0.40 centimeters [Li = 0.40 centimeters], representing the ultimate size achieved under optimal conditions in laboratory-reared populations. Males, in contrast, are substantially smaller and reach a final total length of 0.22 centimeters [Li = 0.22 centimeters], a sexual size dimorphism commonly observed across cladoceran taxa. This difference in asymptotic size is linked to divergent life-history strategies between the sexes, with females investing heavily in brood capacity while males prioritize early maturation and mating opportunities. The total length of 0.25 centimeters [Lp = 0.25 centimeters] recorded at puberty further underscores this pattern, as it is intermediate between the male and female maxima. Growth beyond this point in females is driven largely by the allocation of resources to increasing the volume of the brood chamber, which accommodates larger clutches with each successive adult molt.

Reproduction in Sida crystallina follows a cyclical pattern tightly coupled to the molting rhythm. At 20 °C [T = 20 °C], each female produces 5 eggs per brood [N_R_i = 5 eggs per brood], a fecundity that is maintained across multiple adult instars under favorable feeding regimes. The interval between successive broods is set by the duration of the molting cycle, which lasts 3.9 days per molt, yielding approximately 1.3 broods every 5 days [F_R_i = approximately 1.3 broods every 5 days]. This high output is characteristic of r-selected cladoceran species that colonize ephemeral littoral habitats. Egg production is directly influenced by maternal body size, with larger females in the 0.40 centimeter [Li = 0.40 centimeter] length class consistently carrying the maximum clutch size, whereas smaller or younger adults often produce fewer offspring per brood.

The ecological role of Sida crystallina in freshwater littoral zones is shaped by its relatively large body size compared to other co-occurring cladocerans like Daphnia or Bosmina. Its attachment to submerged macrophytes using a specialized dorsal organ allows it to exploit a microhabitat rich in periphytic algae and detritus. The fast generation time, with a minimum age at birth of 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], enables the species to achieve multiple generations within a single growing season, facilitating rapid population responses to resource pulses. Predation by aquatic insects and young fish exerts strong selective pressure on this species, favoring the relatively large size at birth of 0.034 centimeters [Lb = 0.034 centimeters] as a means of reducing vulnerability to small invertebrate predators. Seasonal shifts in water temperature modulate these life-history traits, and populations at the northern edge of the species range often exhibit slower growth rates and reduced clutch sizes compared to those in temperate lowland lakes.
